title: Rethinking My Desk Job After Chronic Back Pain
script: Narrator: [reflective] For nearly two years, I dismissed the dull ache in my lower back as something that simply came with having an office job.
Narrator: [honest] I told myself that everyone who sits at a desk for eight hours must feel some discomfort, so there was no reason to make a fuss about it.
Narrator: [worried] However, by the time the pain started spreading down my leg, even I could no longer pretend it was ordinary tiredness.
Narrator: [thoughtful] A physiotherapist examined me and explained that, despite feeling fine while sitting, my spine had been under constant pressure for far too long.
Narrator: [surprised] She showed me a diagram of how slouched posture gradually compresses the discs between the vertebrae, which I had never once considered.
Narrator: [determined] If I kept working the way I had been, she warned, the pain would likely return, no matter how many painkillers I relied on.
Narrator: [thoughtful] As a result, I agreed to make several changes, even though I doubted a chair or a desk could really fix something so persistent.
Narrator: [honest] First, I switched to a standing desk for part of the day, which felt awkward and tiring during the first week.
Narrator: [determined] Second, I set a timer to remind myself to stretch every hour, since I tended to forget entirely once I was absorbed in work.
Narrator: [reflective] In spite of my initial doubts, the stretching became the habit that mattered most, more than any equipment I purchased.
Narrator: [honest] There were setbacks, of course; some weeks I skipped the stretches entirely and paid for it with stiffness the next morning.
Narrator: [hopeful] Even so, after about two months, I noticed I could sit through a long meeting without shifting constantly in my seat.
Narrator: [thoughtful] What surprised me most was realizing that pain had quietly shaped my mood, making me irritable in ways I had never connected to my back.
Narrator: [warmly] Now, if I feel the familiar tightness returning, I treat it as a signal rather than something to ignore until it worsens.
Narrator: [reflective] I used to think discomfort was simply the price of a desk job, but I understand now that it was a warning I chose not to hear.
